one_liner: C++ programmable proxy scripted in PipyJS; the vendor's single-core hello-world test shows 1.4-2.6x nginx keep-alive throughput.
what_it_does: Pipy is a single-binary network proxy that works as a stream processor: you write a PipyJS module that chains built-in filters (listen, serveHTTP, demuxHTTP/muxHTTP, connect, acceptTLS, and so on) into pipelines, and each incoming connection gets its own pipeline instance. The same binary covers reverse proxy, sidecar, API gateway, load balancer and protocol converter work (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, TLS, WebSocket, MQTT, Dubbo, Thrift, RESP, SOCKS, PROXY protocol). It is not a drop-in for nginx: configuration is a JavaScript-like program, not nginx.conf, and static files are served from script code through http.File.
how_it_is_fast: It is C++ built on standalone Asio (an epoll/kqueue reactor). Each worker thread owns its own io_context and its own loaded copy of the script, so threads share nothing, and --reuse-port (SO_REUSEPORT, or SO_REUSEPORT_LB on FreeBSD) lets the kernel spread connections across threads. Payload bytes sit in reference-counted 16 KB chunks that are sliced by views, and the HTTP/1 decoder is a hand-written byte-scanning state machine that passes body bytes on as chunk references instead of copying them. Chunks, views and other hot objects come from thread-local per-type free-list pools (pjs::Pool, with an atomic return list for frees from other threads), which keeps malloc off the hot path. PipyJS is an in-house tree-walking interpreter with reference counting and no JIT. In the benchmark the response was a Message built once at load time, so almost no script ran per request.
when_to_use: You want an L4/L7 proxy, sidecar or gateway whose routing, auth and rewriting logic is written as code (JS-like expressions) rather than nginx directives or Lua, shipped as one ~10 MB binary with vendored dependencies.

Small edge, IoT or cheap ARM64 hosts where requests/s per core counts: the vendor's 1-worker test on a 2 vCPU ARM64 VM gave 218,539 vs 82,759 req/s on Ubuntu and 281,176 vs 204,544 on FreeBSD over keep-alive, at about 9.3 MB RSS (nginx 6.5-7.5 MB).
Keep-alive HTTP/1.1 traffic with small messages, where the vendor data also shows a lower saturated p50 (0.45 ms vs 1.20 ms on Ubuntu, 350 us vs 485 us on FreeBSD).
Proxying or converting between several protocols (HTTP/2, TLS, MQTT, Dubbo, Thrift, RESP, SOCKS) from one binary.
Scaling across many cores with --threads=N --reuse-port: the vendor's Pipy 0.90 test went from ~139k req/s on 1 thread to ~1.21M req/s on 12 threads (Xeon Gold 6144, no nginx comparison).
when_not_to_use: As a drop-in nginx web server: nginx.conf is not supported, static files go through script code (http.File), and I found no sendfile() use in Pipy's own src/.
Workloads with one request per connection: in the vendor's ab runs Pipy only ties nginx (59,698 vs 60,824 req/s on Ubuntu, 95,074 vs 93,680 on FreeBSD).
Latency at a fixed request rate: at 10k QPS (fortio) Pipy's p50 on Ubuntu was worse (1.851 ms vs 1.449 ms), and on FreeBSD it tied (506 vs 507 us).

You need Windows binaries or a standard JS runtime: maintainers said in issue #200 that there are no Windows builds, and PipyJS has no classes or prototypes, no BigInt or Symbol, and no npm ecosystem.
You need a large ecosystem or fast-moving project: 832 stars, last release 1.5.14 (2025-09-18), and the 2026 commits are mostly CI, TLS-cipher and admin fixes.

integration.form: standalone executable (proxy server); the CMake options PIPY_STATICLIB and PIPY_SHARED can also build it as a static or shared library
integration.dependencies: Vendored in deps/ and built in: standalone Asio 1.28.0, OpenSSL 3.2.0, zlib 1.3.1, Brotli 1.0.9, LevelDB 1.23, SQLite 3.43.2, yajl 2.1.0, libyaml 0.2.5, libexpat 2.2.6. There are options to use system zlib/OpenSSL or TongSuo. Node.js v12+ is needed only to build the admin GUI.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMake calls cxx_11()); Clang 5.0+ (build.sh defaults CC/CXX to clang); CMake 3.10+ per the README (the docs say 3.0+)
integration.platforms: Linux (RHEL/CentOS, Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, openEuler, OpenWrt, Deepin, Kylin), macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Android; x86-64, ARM64, LoongArch, Hygon. Release binaries: Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS x86-64/aarch64, Android arm64, EL7 RPM. No Windows binaries.
integration.thread_safety: One worker thread by default. --threads=N (up to hardware_concurrency) starts N worker threads, each with its own Asio io_context and its own instance of the script module (shared-nothing). Context variables belong to each pipeline, not to the process. Cross-thread sharing beyond that is not documented in what I read.

gotchas: CMakeLists.txt makes Debug the default build type. build.sh passes Release, but if you call CMake yourself, set -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release or you will benchmark a debug binary.

The defaults are one worker thread and no SO_REUSEPORT. Multi-core throughput needs --threads=N, which the vendor pairs with --reuse-port. Run with no arguments, Pipy starts in repo mode with an admin service/UI on port 6060 (turn it off with --admin-port-off).

The PipyJS reference docs still describe an expression-only language with no if/for/try/class/import, but src/pjs/stmt.hpp implements If/For/Switch/Try/Import/Export statements, so the docs lag the engine. Strings are UTF-8 internally with code-point length ("😀".length is 1).
The third-party list in the LICENSE file (Boost Asio, OpenSSL 1.1.1o/1.1.1g) is out of date: deps/ vendors standalone Asio 1.28.0 and OpenSSL 3.2.0. Check notices yourself when redistributing.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pipy over Pingora when you want proxy logic you can script and hot-reload at runtime from a prebuilt binary, instead of compiling a Rust program against a framework. Pick H2O as an nginx-style origin/static server, and Sogou Workflow or cinatra to embed an HTTP server inside a C++ service; Pipy's niche is programmable proxying and protocol conversion.
verified_claims_summary: In the project's own 2022 wiki test (Pipy version not stated, no compiler flags or CPU model), nginx 1.18.0 (Ubuntu 21) and 1.20.2 (FreeBSD 13) were distro packages with 1 worker, running on the same 2 vCPU ARM64 VM as the client. wrk -c100 -t1 measured Pipy at 218,539 vs 82,759 req/s (2.6x) on Ubuntu and 281,176 vs 204,544 (1.37x) on FreeBSD, with ab short-lived connections a tie. The comparison is not like-for-like: Pipy's replies were ~74 bytes against nginx's ~249 (63-byte vs ~243-byte headers). fortio opened 10,000 sockets for nginx against 100 for Pipy, which fits nginx 1.18's default keepalive_requests of 100 and likely inflates the Ubuntu gap. The FreeBSD Pipy runs used the 8081 echo port (empty body), not the 8080 hello port.
status_note: Active but slow-moving: last release 1.5.14 (2025-09-18) with CI and small fixes into mid-2026. Pipy's own code is MIT; the vendored dependencies keep their own licenses (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Prebuilt Linux and macOS binaries make it easy to try.
